items.stem: What is meant by the mass defect of a nucleus?
options: the difference between the total mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus
the difference between the nucleon number and the proton number
the mass lost when the nucleus emits an α-particle
the mass of the electrons in the atom
items.answer: the difference between the total mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus
items.markingKey: Δm = Zmₚ + (A − Z)mₙ − m(nucleus).

items.stem: Explain why the mass of a nucleus is less than the total mass of its separate nucleons.
items.answer: When nucleons come together energy is released (binding energy); by E = mc² this released energy corresponds to a loss of mass, the mass defect.
items.markingKey: energy released on binding [1]; equivalent mass lost, E = Δmc² [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why energy must be supplied to separate a nucleus into its nucleons.
items.answer: The nucleons are held together by the strong nuclear force; work must be done against it, equal to the binding energy, which reappears as the extra mass of the separate nucleons.
items.markingKey: work against strong force [1]; equals binding energy / mass increases [1] [2]

items.stem: The mass of a ⁷₃Li nucleus is 7.014357 u. The mass of a proton is 1.007276 u and the mass of a neutron is 1.008665 u (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg). Determine the mass defect of the nucleus in u.
items.markingKey: Δm = 3 × 1.007276 + 4 × 1.008665 − 7.014357 = 0.0421 u. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The mass of a ⁹₄Be nucleus is 9.010986 u. The mass of a proton is 1.007276 u and the mass of a neutron is 1.008665 u (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg). Calculate the mass defect in kg and the binding energy in J.

A ⁴₂He nucleus has a mass of 4.001506 u. (proton mass 1.007276 u, neutron mass 1.008665 u, 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) (a) Calculate the mass defect in kg. (b) Calculate the binding energy per nucleon in MeV.
items.markingKey: (a) Δm in u then kg (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.04 × 10⁻²⁹ kg [1] [2] (b) ÷ A and convert (method/substitution) [1]; answer 7.09 MeV with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the definition of the binding energy of a nucleus?
options: the energy released when the nucleus decays
the energy needed to remove one electron
the minimum energy needed to separate the nucleus into its individual protons and neutrons
the kinetic energy of the nucleons
items.answer: the minimum energy needed to separate the nucleus into its individual protons and neutrons
items.markingKey: Binding energy = Δmc².

items.stem: Explain why the binding energy of a nucleus is a positive quantity even though the nucleus has less mass than its parts.
items.answer: Binding energy is defined as the energy that must be supplied to separate the nucleons, so it is positive; the nucleus is in a lower energy state, hence its smaller mass.
items.markingKey: defined as energy supplied to separate [1]; nucleus lower energy/mass [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why energy must be supplied to separate a nucleus into its nucleons. (b) Explain why the mass of a nucleus is less than the total mass of its separate nucleons.
items.answer: (a) The nucleons are held together by the strong nuclear force; work must be done against it, equal to the binding energy, which reappears as the extra mass of the separate nucleons. (b) When nucleons come together energy is released (binding energy); by E = mc² this released energy corresponds to a loss of mass, the mass defect.
items.markingKey: (a) work against strong force [1]; equals binding energy / mass increases [1] [2] (b) energy released on binding [1]; equivalent mass lost, E = Δmc² [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the mass of a nucleus is less than the total mass of its separate nucleons. (b) Explain why energy must be supplied to separate a nucleus into its nucleons.
items.answer: (a) When nucleons come together energy is released (binding energy); by E = mc² this released energy corresponds to a loss of mass, the mass defect. (b) The nucleons are held together by the strong nuclear force; work must be done against it, equal to the binding energy, which reappears as the extra mass of the separate nucleons.
items.markingKey: (a) energy released on binding [1]; equivalent mass lost, E = Δmc² [1] [2] (b) work against strong force [1]; equals binding energy / mass increases [1] [2]

items.stem: A 60 W lamp operates for one year (3.16 × 10⁷ s). Work out the mass equivalent of the energy used.
items.markingKey: Δm = ΔE/c² = 1.90 × 10⁹/(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.11 × 10⁻⁸ kg. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.markingKey: Δm = ΔE/c² = 1.90 × 10⁹/(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.11 × 10⁻⁸ kg. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [3]

items.answer: (a) Minimum energy needed to separate a nucleus into its separate nucleons. (b) 3 protons, 4 neutrons (c) 6.29 × 10⁻¹² J

items.answer: (a) Minimum energy needed to separate a nucleus into its separate nucleons. (b) 8.77 × 10⁻²⁸ kg (c) 7.90 × 10⁻¹¹ J

items.stem: Which nuclide has the highest binding energy per nucleon?
items.answer: iron-56
items.markingKey: The peak of the BE/nucleon curve is near A = 56–62.

items.stem: Use the binding energy per nucleon curve to explain why both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy.
items.answer: Iron-56 is at the peak. Heavy nuclei splitting and light nuclei joining both produce nuclei closer to the peak, with higher binding energy per nucleon; total binding energy increases, so energy is released (mass decreases).
items.markingKey: products nearer the peak / higher BE per nucleon [1]; increase in total BE released as energy [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why binding energy per nucleon, rather than total binding energy, indicates the stability of a nucleus.
items.answer: Total binding energy grows with the number of nucleons; dividing by A gives the average energy holding each nucleon, so nuclei can be compared: higher BE per nucleon means more tightly bound and more stable.
items.markingKey: total BE increases with A [1]; per nucleon allows comparison of stability [1] [2]

items.stem: In a fission reaction, a Pu-239 nucleus (binding energy per nucleon 7.56 MeV) absorbs a neutron and splits into Xe-134 (8.41 MeV) and Zr-103 (8.57 MeV), releasing 3 neutrons. The values in brackets are binding energies per nucleon. Calculate the energy released in MeV.
items.answer: 203 MeV
items.markingKey: E = 134 × 8.41 + 103 × 8.57 − 239 × 7.56 = 203 MeV. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In a fission reaction, a U-235 nucleus (binding energy per nucleon 7.59 MeV) absorbs a neutron and splits into Ba-144 (8.27 MeV) and Kr-89 (8.62 MeV), releasing 3 neutrons. The values in brackets are binding energies per nucleon. Calculate the energy released in one fission, in MeV and in J.
items.markingKey: total BE of products [1]; minus BE of U = 174 MeV [1]; × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 2.79 × 10⁻¹¹ J [1] [3]

items.stem: Arjun is revising the graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number, which rises steeply to a peak of about 8.8 MeV near A = 56 and falls to about 7.59 MeV for uranium-235. (a) Explain, using the graph, why fission of uranium-235 releases energy. (b) Explain why iron-56 cannot release energy by fission or fusion. (c) State one difference between fission and fusion.
items.answer: (a) The products (A ≈ 90–140) have higher BE per nucleon (≈ 8.3 MeV) than uranium-235 (7.59 MeV), so total BE increases. (b) It is at the peak; any change gives nuclei with lower BE per nucleon, which would require energy input. (c) Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei (fusion needs very high temperature; fission is started by neutrons).
items.markingKey: (a) products higher BE per nucleon [1]; total BE increases, energy released [1] [2] (b) It is at the peak; any change gives nuclei with lower BE per nucleon, which would require energy input [1] (c) Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei (fusion needs very high temperature; fission is started by neutrons) [1]

items.stem: Energy is released in nuclear fission because …
options: the products have a lower binding energy per nucleon
the products have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the original nucleus
the neutrons have a large kinetic energy initially
items.answer: the products have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the original nucleus
items.markingKey: Products are more tightly bound; total BE increases.

items.stem: Explain why fusion reactions are difficult to achieve on Earth.
items.answer: Nuclei are positively charged and repel; extremely high temperatures (~10⁸ K) and pressures/densities are needed so that they collide with enough kinetic energy to get within range of the strong force, and the hot plasma must be contained.
items.markingKey: electrostatic repulsion [1]; very high temperature and containment needed [1] [2]

items.stem: A fusion reaction is ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n. Data: nuclear masses: ²₁H 2.013553 u, ³₁H 3.015501 u, ³₂He 3.014932 u, ⁴₂He 4.001506 u, ¹₀n 1.008665 u, ¹₁p 1.007276 u. Calculate the energy released in the reaction in MeV.
items.answer: 17.6 MeV
items.markingKey: Δm = 0.01888 u [1]; E = Δmc² with Δm in kg [1]; = 17.6 MeV [1] [3]

items.stem: A fusion reaction is ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₁H + ¹₁p. Data: nuclear masses: ²₁H 2.013553 u, ³₁H 3.015501 u, ³₂He 3.014932 u, ⁴₂He 4.001506 u, ¹₀n 1.008665 u, ¹₁p 1.007276 u. Calculate the energy released in the reaction in MeV.
items.answer: 4.04 MeV
items.markingKey: Δm = 0.004329 u [1]; E = Δmc² with Δm in kg [1]; = 4.04 MeV [1] [3]

items.stem: A physics textbook used in Riyadh shows the graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number, which rises steeply to a peak of about 8.8 MeV near A = 56 and falls to about 7.59 MeV for uranium-235. (a) Estimate the energy released when a uranium-235 nucleus splits into two nuclei each with BE per nucleon 8.3 MeV (ignore free neutrons). (b) Explain why iron-56 cannot release energy by fission or fusion. (c) State one difference between fission and fusion.
items.answer: (a) 167 MeV (b) It is at the peak; any change gives nuclei with lower BE per nucleon, which would require energy input. (c) Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei (fusion needs very high temperature; fission is started by neutrons).

items.stem: What is meant by the activity of a radioactive sample?
options: the time for half the nuclei to decay
the energy of each emitted particle
the number of nuclei decaying per unit time
items.answer: the number of nuclei decaying per unit time
items.markingKey: A = −dN/dt = λN, unit Bq.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the random and spontaneous nature of radioactive decay.
items.answer: Random: it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when; each has a constant probability per unit time. Spontaneous: the decay is not affected by external conditions such as temperature, pressure or chemical state.
items.markingKey: random explained [1]; spontaneous explained [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how fluctuations in the count rate from a radioactive source provide evidence for the random nature of decay.
items.answer: Repeated counts over equal time intervals vary about a mean, because the number of nuclei decaying in each interval is a matter of chance.
items.markingKey: count varies about mean [1]; decay of each nucleus a matter of chance [1] [2]

items.stem: The half-life of phosphorus-32 is 14.3 days (1.24 × 10⁶ s). Work out the decay constant.
items.markingKey: λ = ln 2/t½ = 0.693/1.24 × 10⁶ = 5.61 × 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A sample contains 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ kg of iodine-131, half-life 8.02 days (6.93 × 10⁵ s). Calculate the decay constant and the activity of the sample. (mass of one nucleus ≈ 131 u)

A source of iodine-131 (half-life 8.02 days) has an activity of 1.0 × 10⁸ Bq. (a) Calculate the decay constant in s⁻¹. (b) Calculate the number of undecayed iodine-131 nuclei. (c) Calculate the mass of iodine-131 present (mass of one nucleus ≈ 131 u).

A sample of radon-222 (half-life 3.82 days) has an initial activity of 4.0 × 10⁵ Bq. (a) Calculate the decay constant in s⁻¹. (b) State the activity after three half-lives. (c) Explain why the activity, rather than the number of nuclei, is measured in practice.
items.answer: (a) 2.10 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹ (b) 5.00 × 10⁴ Bq (c) Decays (emissions) can be counted with a detector; undecayed nuclei cannot be counted directly.
items.markingKey: (a) λ = ln 2/t½ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.10 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) A₀/8: 5.00 × 10⁴ Bq [1] (c) Decays (emissions) can be counted with a detector; undecayed nuclei cannot be counted directly [1]

items.stem: A sample of cobalt-60 (half-life 5.27 years) has an initial activity of 4.0 × 10⁵ Bq. (a) Calculate the decay constant in s⁻¹. (b) Calculate the initial number of undecayed nuclei. (c) State the activity after three half-lives.
items.markingKey: (a) λ = ln 2/t½ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.16 × 10⁻⁹ s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) N = A/λ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 9.61 × 10¹³ [1] [2] (c) A₀/8: 5.00 × 10⁴ Bq [1]

items.stem: The decay constant λ is …
options: the time for the activity to halve
the number of decays per second
the probability per unit time that a nucleus will decay
items.answer: the probability per unit time that a nucleus will decay
items.markingKey: λ = A/N.

items.stem: A nuclide has a half-life of 10 minutes. What is its decay constant?
Derive the relationship λ = ln 2/t½.
items.answer: N = N₀e^(−λt); at t = t½, N = N₀/2: ½ = e^(−λt½), so ln 2 = λt½.
items.markingKey: substitute N = N₀/2 [1]; take logs [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a radioactive source used as a medical tracer should have a half-life of a few hours.
items.answer: Long enough to be prepared, injected and measured during the procedure, but short enough that the activity (and dose to the patient) falls quickly afterwards.
items.markingKey: long enough for procedure [1]; short to limit dose [1] [2]

items.stem: A student records the counts from a long-lived radioactive source in five successive 10 s intervals: 242, 223, 198, 233, 187. The background count is 3 per 10 s. Explain why the counts differ and how the student should obtain the best value for the count rate due to the source.
items.answer: Decay is random, so the number of decays in equal intervals fluctuates about a mean. Take the mean (217 per 10 s), subtract background and divide by 10 s (or count for a longer time).
items.markingKey: random nature of decay [1]; mean and subtract background; longer counting time reduces percentage fluctuation [1] [3]

items.answer: A₀/16

items.stem: Explain why a graph of ln(activity) against time is used to find the half-life of a source.
items.answer: ln A = ln A₀ − λt gives a straight line of gradient −λ, which can be measured accurately using all the data; t½ = ln 2/λ.
items.markingKey: straight line, gradient −λ [1]; t½ = ln 2/λ [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the number of nuclei decaying per second falls as time passes.
items.answer: Activity A = λN; λ is constant, but N decreases as nuclei decay, so A decreases in proportion to the remaining N.
items.markingKey: A = λN [1]; N decreases [1] [2]

items.stem: A sample of strontium-90 (half-life 28.8 years) has an initial activity of 1200 Bq. Calculate the activity after 66.2 years.
items.answer: 244 Bq
items.markingKey: A = A₀e^(−λt) = A₀(½)^(t/t½) = 1200 × 0.5^2.3 = 244 Bq. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.markingKey: (a) All decay exponentially with the same λ. (b) 24 h = 4 half-lives.

items.stem: Explain how radiocarbon dating uses the exponential decay law.
items.answer: Living organisms keep a constant ratio of C-14 to C-12; after death C-14 decays with t½ = 5730 y. Measuring the present activity per gram and comparing with that of living material gives t from A = A₀e^(−λt).
items.markingKey: constant ratio while alive, decay after death [1]; t = ln(A₀/A)/λ [1] [2]

items.stem: The mass of a ²³⁵₉₂U nucleus is 234.993422 u. The mass of a proton is 1.007276 u and the mass of a neutron is 1.008665 u (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg). Calculate the mass defect in kg and the binding energy in J.

A ¹²₆C nucleus has a mass of 11.996709 u. (proton mass 1.007276 u, neutron mass 1.008665 u, 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) (a) Define binding energy. (b) Calculate the mass defect in kg. (c) Calculate the binding energy per nucleon in MeV.
items.answer: (a) Minimum energy needed to separate a nucleus into its separate nucleons. (b) 1.64 × 10⁻²⁸ kg (c) 7.70 MeV
items.markingKey: (a) Minimum energy needed to separate a nucleus into its separate nucleons [1] (b) Δm in u then kg (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.64 × 10⁻²⁸ kg [1] [2] (c) ÷ A and convert (method/substitution) [1]; answer 7.70 MeV with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Fusion of light nuclei releases energy because …
options: the binding energy per nucleon increases
the binding energy per nucleon decreases
items.answer: the binding energy per nucleon increases
items.markingKey: Moving up the curve towards iron.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why fusion reactions are difficult to achieve on Earth. (b) Use the binding energy per nucleon curve to explain why both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy.
items.answer: (a) Nuclei are positively charged and repel; extremely high temperatures (~10⁸ K) and pressures/densities are needed so that they collide with enough kinetic energy to get within range of the strong force, and the hot plasma must be contained. (b) Iron-56 is at the peak. Heavy nuclei splitting and light nuclei joining both produce nuclei closer to the peak, with higher binding energy per nucleon; total binding energy increases, so energy is released (mass decreases).
items.markingKey: (a) electrostatic repulsion [1]; very high temperature and containment needed [1] [2] (b) products nearer the peak / higher BE per nucleon [1]; increase in total BE released as energy [1] [2]

items.stem: In a fission reaction, a U-235 nucleus (binding energy per nucleon 7.59 MeV) absorbs a neutron and splits into Ba-144 (8.27 MeV) and Kr-89 (8.62 MeV), releasing 3 neutrons. The values in brackets are binding energies per nucleon. Determine the energy released in MeV.
items.answer: 174 MeV
items.markingKey: E = 144 × 8.27 + 89 × 8.62 − 235 × 7.59 = 174 MeV. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In a fission reaction, a U-235 nucleus (binding energy per nucleon 7.59 MeV) absorbs a neutron and splits into Xe-140 (8.29 MeV) and Sr-94 (8.59 MeV), releasing 2 neutrons. The values in brackets are binding energies per nucleon. Calculate the energy released in one fission, in MeV and in J.
items.markingKey: total BE of products [1]; minus BE of U = 184 MeV [1]; × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 2.95 × 10⁻¹¹ J [1] [3]

items.stem: An energy researcher in Mexico City compares the graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number, which rises steeply to a peak of about 8.8 MeV near A = 56 and falls to about 7.56 MeV for plutonium-239. (a) Define binding energy per nucleon. (b) Explain, using the graph, why fission of plutonium-239 releases energy. (c) Explain why iron-56 cannot release energy by fission or fusion. (d) The binding energies per nucleon are 1.11 MeV for ²₁H and 7.07 MeV for ⁴₂He. Estimate the energy released when two ²₁H nuclei fuse to form one ⁴₂He nucleus.
items.answer: (a) Total binding energy of a nucleus divided by the number of nucleons. (b) The products (A ≈ 90–140) have higher BE per nucleon (≈ 8.5 MeV) than plutonium-239 (7.56 MeV), so total BE increases. (c) It is at the peak; any change gives nuclei with lower BE per nucleon, which would require energy input. (d) 23.8 MeV
items.markingKey: (a) Total binding energy of a nucleus divided by the number of nucleons [1] (b) products higher BE per nucleon [1]; total BE increases, energy released [1] [2] (c) It is at the peak; any change gives nuclei with lower BE per nucleon, which would require energy input [1] (d) 4 × 7.07 − 4 × BE per nucleon of ²₁H (method/substitution) [1]; answer 23.8 MeV with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Radioactive decay is described as random because … (b) Define half-life.
items.answer: (a) it is not possible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay (b) The time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei (or the activity) of a nuclide to fall to half its initial value.
items.markingKey: (a) Each nucleus has a constant probability of decay per unit time. (b) time for N or A to halve [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Derive the relationship λ = ln 2/t½. (b) Explain what is meant by the random and spontaneous nature of radioactive decay.
items.answer: (a) N = N₀e^(−λt); at t = t½, N = N₀/2: ½ = e^(−λt½), so ln 2 = λt½. (b) Random: it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when; each has a constant probability per unit time. Spontaneous: the decay is not affected by external conditions such as temperature, pressure or chemical state.
items.markingKey: (a) substitute N = N₀/2 [1]; take logs [1] [2] (b) random explained [1]; spontaneous explained [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how fluctuations in the count rate from a radioactive source provide evidence for the random nature of decay. (b) Explain what is meant by the random and spontaneous nature of radioactive decay.
items.answer: (a) Repeated counts over equal time intervals vary about a mean, because the number of nuclei decaying in each interval is a matter of chance. (b) Random: it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when; each has a constant probability per unit time. Spontaneous: the decay is not affected by external conditions such as temperature, pressure or chemical state.
items.markingKey: (a) count varies about mean [1]; decay of each nucleus a matter of chance [1] [2] (b) random explained [1]; spontaneous explained [1] [2]

items.stem: The half-life of iodine-131 is 8.02 days (6.93 × 10⁵ s). Determine the decay constant.
items.markingKey: λ = ln 2/t½ = 0.693/6.93 × 10⁵ = 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The half-life of americium-241 is 432 years (1.37 × 10¹⁰ s). Work out the decay constant.
items.markingKey: λ = ln 2/t½ = 0.693/1.37 × 10¹⁰ = 5.08 × 10⁻¹¹ s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A sample of cobalt-60 (half-life 5.27 years) has an initial activity of 2.0 × 10⁶ Bq. (a) Calculate the decay constant in s⁻¹. (b) State the activity after three half-lives. (c) Explain why the activity, rather than the number of nuclei, is measured in practice.
items.answer: (a) 4.16 × 10⁻⁹ s⁻¹ (b) 2.50 × 10⁵ Bq (c) Decays (emissions) can be counted with a detector; undecayed nuclei cannot be counted directly.
items.markingKey: (a) λ = ln 2/t½ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.16 × 10⁻⁹ s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) A₀/8: 2.50 × 10⁵ Bq [1] (c) Decays (emissions) can be counted with a detector; undecayed nuclei cannot be counted directly [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how radiocarbon dating uses the exponential decay law. (b) Explain why the number of nuclei decaying per second falls as time passes.
items.answer: (a) Living organisms keep a constant ratio of C-14 to C-12; after death C-14 decays with t½ = 5730 y. Measuring the present activity per gram and comparing with that of living material gives t from A = A₀e^(−λt). (b) Activity A = λN; λ is constant, but N decreases as nuclei decay, so A decreases in proportion to the remaining N.
items.markingKey: (a) constant ratio while alive, decay after death [1]; t = ln(A₀/A)/λ [1] [2] (b) A = λN [1]; N decreases [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how radiocarbon dating uses the exponential decay law. (b) Explain why a graph of ln(activity) against time is used to find the half-life of a source.
items.answer: (a) Living organisms keep a constant ratio of C-14 to C-12; after death C-14 decays with t½ = 5730 y. Measuring the present activity per gram and comparing with that of living material gives t from A = A₀e^(−λt). (b) ln A = ln A₀ − λt gives a straight line of gradient −λ, which can be measured accurately using all the data; t½ = ln 2/λ.
items.markingKey: (a) constant ratio while alive, decay after death [1]; t = ln(A₀/A)/λ [1] [2] (b) straight line, gradient −λ [1]; t½ = ln 2/λ [1] [2]

items.stem: The corrected count rate from a radioactive source falls from 1500 counts per minute to 842 counts per minute in 5.0 hours. Calculate the decay constant and the half-life of the source.

items.answer: (a) 3.20 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ (b) 1.56 × 10¹³ (c) Activity falls quickly after the scan, reducing the dose to the patient.

items.stem: A mass defect of 1 u corresponds to an energy of approximately …
items.answer: 930 MeV

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the mass of a nucleus is less than the total mass of its separate nucleons. (b) Explain why energy must be supplied to separate a nucleus into its nucleons.
items.answer: (a) When nucleons come together energy is released (binding energy); by E = mc² this released energy corresponds to a loss of mass, the mass defect. (b) The nucleons are held together by the strong nuclear force; work must be done against it, equal to the binding energy, which reappears as the extra mass of the separate nucleons.
items.markingKey: (a) energy released on binding [1]; equivalent mass lost, E = Δmc² [1] [2] (b) work against strong force [1]; equals binding energy / mass increases [1] [2]

items.stem: A nuclear power station produces 1.2 × 10⁹ W of electrical power at an efficiency of 33%. Work out the rate at which mass is converted to energy in the reactor.
items.markingKey: Δm = ΔE/c² = 3.64 × 10⁹/(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 4.04 × 10⁻⁸ kg s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Freya is revising the graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number, which rises steeply to a peak of about 8.8 MeV near A = 56 and falls to about 7.59 MeV for uranium-235. (a) Estimate the energy released when a uranium-235 nucleus splits into two nuclei each with BE per nucleon 8.4 MeV (ignore free neutrons). (b) Explain why iron-56 cannot release energy by fission or fusion. (c) The binding energies per nucleon are 1.11 MeV for ²₁H and 7.07 MeV for ⁴₂He. Estimate the energy released when two ²₁H nuclei fuse to form one ⁴₂He nucleus. (d) State one difference between fission and fusion.
items.answer: (a) 190 MeV (b) It is at the peak; any change gives nuclei with lower BE per nucleon, which would require energy input. (c) 23.8 MeV (d) Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei (fusion needs very high temperature; fission is started by neutrons).
